notes: Demanding path. The need names two designs (a cross-sectional survey and a retrospective records review), so routing is unresolved at create and the problem reply returns family null (family unchanged, basis unresolved). The fixture search returns seven records; one undated service report has year null and the appraisal leaves it without grade or method score (it stays 'unrated' with null scores, never 2020, 50 or 'low'). The Design stage resolves the family to cross-sectional. Its decision rests on ledger claims c1, c2 and c4, but the model marks the ethics gate 'met' with no evidence: the gate is resolved to 'unknown' with an issue (holds at 875fe59 in applyDecision), so acceptance is allowed (a supported selection) while the action stays blocked, and it stays blocked after reload, reopen and in the export because nothing ever supplies the ethics decision. The problem reply restates the typed constraints verbatim, so G11 leaves them unchanged with no rejected-change issue. Record ids are stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts, computed by the generator: DOI-based for records 1, 3, 4, 6, 7 (ev-1ouzx7v, ev-1kpf7p0, ev-0qp4o82, ev-0uhs1nc, ev-10nu9sn); title and year for record 2 (ev-1a3srca) and title with an unknown year for record 5 (ev-0pk9zqe). Requires D2 (null family leaves basis unresolved), S13 (appraisal dispatch), S11 (routing, recommendedFamily, selectionStatus, actionStatus, family set on acceptance) and D5 (decision status text). inputs.need:
I am a pelvic health physiotherapist and lead the women's health physiotherapy service at a teaching hospital. We run six-week group classes in pelvic floor muscle training for women with stress urinary incontinence, both after childbirth and in midlife, because group classes let us see far more women than one-to-one appointments. The problem is attendance. Of the 1,100 or so women referred to us last year, fewer than half came to the first class and only about a quarter came to four or more of the six sessions. The women who do not come are not a random group: from the referral letters it looks as if younger mothers, women who live far from the hospital and women who need an interpreter drop out most, but that is an impression, not data.

Before we change anything, I want to understand what is associated with attending and what stops women from coming. I cannot decide between a cross-sectional survey of women referred in the last year and a retrospective review of our referral and attendance records, and I suspect we need some of both. We have no research funding. The service manager can cover printing and postage, and our administrator could help with mailing. The survey would need translation into at least two languages besides English. I have not yet asked the hospital research ethics board whether a survey of patients who did not attend needs full review, and I am unsure whether we are allowed to link survey answers to attendance records.
inputs.constraints: No research funding; printing and postage up to 1,500 from the service budget. Survey materials in English and the two most common other languages of referred women. No extra clinic appointments for the study.

records.title: Attendance at group pelvic floor muscle training for stress urinary incontinence: a systematic review of adherence and its predictors
records.authors: Lindahl-Okafor B, Pritchard-Menon S, Vasquez-Aarts H
records.abstract: We reviewed 26 studies reporting attendance at group pelvic floor muscle training for women with stress urinary incontinence. In trials, women attended a median of 78 percent of sessions, but in the nine studies of routine services only 30 to 52 percent of referred women attended more than half of the sessions. Longer travel time, caring responsibilities and milder symptoms were the predictors most often reported, while group size and instructor were rarely studied. Most studies measured attendance from service records and predictors from referral data, and none linked patient-reported barriers to recorded attendance.

records.title: Non-attendance at postnatal pelvic floor physiotherapy classes: a retrospective review of 1,204 referrals
records.abstract: We reviewed the records of 1,204 women referred to postnatal pelvic floor classes at one hospital over two years. Forty-one percent attended the first session and 23 percent attended four or more of six sessions. Non-attendance was more common in women aged under 25, in women living more than 20 kilometres from the hospital and in women whose records noted an interpreter need. Referral by a midwife rather than a doctor was not associated with attendance. Reasons for non-attendance were not recorded, and the review could not separate women who chose not to attend from those who could not.

records.title: Why women do not come: a postal survey of barriers to pelvic floor classes among referred women
records.authors: Harrington-Oduya P, Salgado-Lind M, Chen-Abara R
records.abstract: We mailed a questionnaire to 860 women referred to group pelvic floor classes in one year; 327 replied (38 percent). Childcare was the most common barrier (46 percent), followed by embarrassment about discussing symptoms in a group (31 percent) and class times that clashed with work (29 percent). Non-attenders were less likely to reply than attenders (24 against 55 percent), so barriers among non-attenders are probably underestimated. Answers were not linked to attendance records, and the questionnaire was offered in English only.

records.title: Evening and online pelvic floor classes and first-session attendance in a hospital physiotherapy service: a before-after comparison
records.abstract: A hospital service added two evening classes and one live online class each week to its daytime group programme. Comparing 12 months before and after, first-session attendance rose from 44 to 63 percent and completion of four or more sessions from 26 to 37 percent. The rise was largest among women with children under five. Waiting time fell over the same period, which may explain part of the change, and the service did not collect reasons for non-attendance. Women attending online reported more technical problems in the first month, and women without home internet access used the evening classes instead.

records.title: Pelvic floor class attendance across a regional physiotherapy network: service report
records.abstract: This internal report summarises attendance at group pelvic floor classes in five hospital physiotherapy services. Completion of four or more sessions ranged from 19 to 44 percent between services. Services offering childcare-friendly times reported higher completion, but the report does not describe how attendance was counted, which months were included or how services were chosen. No statistical comparison was made, and the report carries no date, so it can only suggest where differences between services might lie. It was prepared for a network planning day and has not been reviewed outside the network.

records.title: Language, interpreters and attendance at women's health physiotherapy: a cross-sectional study
records.authors: Kaur-Ellison S, Mbatha-Frost D, Olsen-Achebe T
records.abstract: Using referral and attendance records for 2,310 women referred to women's health physiotherapy in two hospitals, we compared attendance by recorded language needs. Women who needed an interpreter were about half as likely to attend their first appointment (prevalence ratio 0.52, 95 percent CI 0.41 to 0.66) after adjustment for age and distance. Group classes had lower attendance than individual appointments for women needing an interpreter, and no class offered interpretation. Interpreter need was recorded inconsistently, so some women with limited English were probably classed as not needing one.

records.title: Group versus individual pelvic floor muscle training: adherence in a randomised comparison
records.abstract: We randomly allocated 248 women with stress urinary incontinence to six weekly group classes or to individual sessions with the same exercises. Attendance at four or more sessions was similar (71 percent group, 74 percent individual), and improvement in leakage episodes did not differ at three months. Trial participants were volunteers who lived near the hospital, so attendance was much higher than in routine services. The group format cost less per woman treated. Women in the group arm said that meeting others with the same problem made it easier to keep going, although three withdrew because of the class times.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; one undated service report is left unrated. Attendance at group pelvic floor classes in routine services is far below trial attendance, and records-based studies point to age, distance and interpreter need, while surveys point to childcare, embarrassment and class times. Nobody has linked reported barriers to recorded attendance, and surveys miss non-attenders. Evening and online classes were followed by higher attendance in one service, but waiting times fell at the same time.
response.gradeRationale: Single-service observational studies and one survey with low response; consistent direction for distance, language and childcare but serious risk of bias and indirect trial evidence.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised, one undated report unrated; five source-derived claims; overall certainty low.

response.reading: Attendance depends on factors visible in records (age, distance, interpreter need; claims c1 and c4) and on barriers that only women can report (childcare, embarrassment, timing; claim c2). No study has joined the two (claim c5), and surveys lose exactly the women who do not attend. Class timing looks modifiable (claim c3). The service's question is therefore cross-sectional: which factors, reported and recorded, go with attendance among all women referred in one year.

response.overview: Cross-sectional study of all women referred to group pelvic floor classes in one year: booking records for everyone, a translated barrier survey, and linkage of answers to attendance for women who consent.

response.designSummary: Cross-sectional analysis of all referrals for recorded factors, and of linked respondents for reported barriers.
response.sampleSize: All 1,112 referrals enter the records analysis; with about 25 percent completing four or more sessions, a factor present in 20 percent of women gives about 80 percent power to detect a prevalence ratio of 0.65 (two-sided alpha 0.05). With a 40 percent response (about 445 linked respondents) and completion of about 35 percent among respondents, a barrier reported by 40 percent of respondents gives about 80 percent power for a prevalence ratio of about 0.7; a barrier's prevalence is estimated within about 4.6 percentage points.
response.primaryAnalysis: Poisson regression with robust variance for completion, giving prevalence ratios for age band, distance band and interpreter need in all referrals; for linked respondents, the same model adds childcare, embarrassment and timing barriers, weighted for nonresponse.
response.secondaryAnalysis: The same models for first-session attendance; response by attendance and language; preferences for evening and online classes among non-attenders.
response.missingData: Missing survey items below 10 percent are handled by multiple imputation within respondents; non-response is addressed by inverse probability weights built from recorded factors.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; six pre-specified factors reported with confidence intervals and no stepwise selection.
response.software: R; weights and models fixed in an analysis plan before the survey closes.
overfittingGuards: Weights built only from recorded factors
response.summary: All referrals for recorded factors, about 445 linked respondents for barriers; prevalence ratios with robust variance.

response.risks: Low: a mailed questionnaire about continence and barriers. Risks are distress or embarrassment and contact with women who chose not to attend; nobody is contacted twice after declining.
response.consent: Returning the questionnaire indicates consent to the survey; a separate tick box records consent to link answers to the booking record, and answers are not linked without it.
response.data: Names and addresses are used only by the administrator for mailing; linked analysis files hold a study number and no names; files are kept on the hospital research drive and deleted five years after publication.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: language, age, distance, caring responsibilities and income shape both attendance and response. The survey is translated into the two most common other languages with interpreter-supported telephone completion, and results are reported by language group and distance band.
response.effectiveness: Useful if it shows which barriers are common among non-attenders and which are modifiable.
response.efficiency: Existing records and a short survey; no new clinic contact.
response.costs: Printing and postage up to 1,500 from budget line WHP-26-09; staff time within existing roles.
response.grants: None needed; a positive redesign could seek charitable funding for evening classes.
response.partnerships: Two women from the service's patient group review the questionnaire; midwifery and primary care referrers are informed.
response.rebPath: The hospital research ethics board has not yet decided whether the survey of non-attenders and the linkage need full review; the study does not start until it has. ICH-GCP and Declaration of Helsinki principles apply to consent and confidentiality.
response.limitations: Nonresponse among non-attenders, recall of barriers up to a year after referral, and inconsistent recording of interpreter need.
response.summary: Low-risk linked survey with separate consent for linkage; the ethics board decision is still pending.

response.title: Factors associated with completing group pelvic floor muscle training among referred women: a cross-sectional study linking booking records and a translated survey
response.abstract: Objective: to identify recorded factors and reported barriers associated with completing four or more sessions of group pelvic floor training. Design: cross-sectional study of all women referred in one year, with booking records for everyone and a translated survey linked to attendance with consent. Results and conclusions will be written after analysis.
response.introduction: Group pelvic floor training works when women attend, but routine services see far lower attendance than trials, and no study has linked women's reported barriers to their recorded attendance.
response.methods: All 1,112 referrals between September 2025 and August 2026 were included. Recorded factors and attendance were extracted from booking records; a 20-item survey in three languages with two reminders asked about barriers, and answers were linked to records with consent. Prevalence ratios came from Poisson models with robust variance, weighted for nonresponse.

response.discussion: The discussion will separate modifiable barriers from fixed factors, weigh nonresponse among non-attenders, and state which class changes the findings support testing.
response.limitations: Nonresponse, recall, inconsistent interpreter recording and one service.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will describe associations, not the effect of any change to the classes.
